dict.string: Opens the app straight to the settings menu. Useful if you changed anything there and need to change it back but the app won't start.

Lets iSH-AOK move cold guest memory out to storage, so a large mostly-idle heap or a background process tree stops counting against the memory iOS allows the app. It will not make a working set that is genuinely too big run well.
Off unless you turn it on: swapping writes to the device's flash, and the swap area takes up that much space in the app's container while it exists. Both settings take effect the next time iSH-AOK starts, and swap stays off until you have chosen a size as well as switched it on.
The sizes offered here do not know how much room this device actually has. If there is not enough free space for the size you pick, iSH-AOK leaves swap off rather than quietly making a smaller area than you asked for; "cat /proc/ish/swap" in the guest says which of those happened.

Save the whole session when iSH-AOK goes to the background, and bring it back on the next launch. iOS ends this app routinely -- memory pressure, or a swipe away -- and without this that always loses the session.
Off by default, because it spends storage and is not free of limits. A session running something iSH-AOK cannot describe is not saved: it says so, and the next launch starts normally. "cat /proc/ish/checkpoint" in the guest reports what the last attempt did and, if it refused, why.

Swap to a USB drive instead of the app's container. Writes go to a .aok-swap file on the drive, keeping internal flash wear-free. Turn this on, then pick the drive in the app the next time it launches.
Warning: exFAT drives (most USB sticks) cannot guarantee preallocated space. If the drive fills up while swap is active, affected guest processes will crash. Use a drive with plenty of free space, or format it as APFS if possible.
If the drive is pulled while swap is active, evicted pages that touch it will fail -- the guest stays running but those processes may crash. Turn this off before removing the drive.

Holds cold memory compressed in RAM instead of writing it to storage. Measured 2.2–2.8x on real workloads, so a 128 MB pool holds roughly 300 MB of guest memory, and a page comes back about two orders of magnitude faster than a read from flash.
Works on its own — Swap is NOT required, and with Swap off nothing is ever written to storage at all. If Swap is also on, this sits in front of it and only what does not compress reaches the file.
Uses the RAM you give it, and it counts against the same memory limit the guest does — so a pool bigger than the device can spare makes things worse, not better. Anything above a quarter of this device's memory is reduced to that.
